passage: Chetan, you've been sulking at your desk all morning, and I think I know why. You call me Saurabh sir and think I've always had it together. Let me tell you what I learnt at your age. I was twenty-five, newly married, and I went silent after every fight with your Bhabhi. Sometimes for days. She thought I hated her. One night, after a week of it, I sat on the edge of the bed and forced the words out: "When I go quiet, it's because I'm overwhelmed. It's not that I don't care. Can I take half an hour, and then come back and talk?" She stared at me as if I'd grown a second head. Then she said, "Why didn't you ever tell me that?" After that, my silence meant something else. A pause, not a punishment.

Four days of frozen politeness in their Kolkata flat, and then, on Saturday morning, Vaibhav put two cups of tea on the table and sat down across from Bidisha.
"Can I explain something?" he said. His hands were around the cup. "When we fight and I go quiet, it's not that I don't care. I get flooded. My head fills up and I'm scared I'll say something cruel."
Bidisha didn't answer at once. She had spent four days thinking the silence was aimed at her.
"So next time," Vaibhav went on, "can I say, 'I need twenty minutes,' and then come back and finish it? I will come back."
Bidisha breathed out. "If you tell me that, I can wait."

qa.a: By explaining that he goes quiet when flooded, not because he doesn't care, and asking for a short break with a promised return, he turned silence from a weapon into a signal.

I remember exactly where I was standing when I broke the ice with Pradeep: by the washing machine, holding a wet towel.
We'd been in a freeze for a week after our fight about his mother's visit. I was the silent one. I always was, even as a little girl.
That day I said, "I need to tell you something. When I go quiet, it's not because I don't care. I get overwhelmed, and I'm scared of saying something I'll regret."
Pradeep stared at me. "I thought you were trying to punish me."
"I know. Can I tell you next time? Say I need a break, and then come back to it?"
He nodded slowly. I'm Tanuja, and that towel dried on the line as the first real talk we'd had in weeks began.

qa.a: A wet towel, by the washing machine.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she explained her silence?
qa.a: Tanuja felt nervous and exposed but determined to explain that the silence came from being overwhelmed and scared, not from not caring.

qa.q: What turning point did Tanuja create?
qa.a: By explaining her silence and asking to name a break and come back, she turned the silence from a punishment into a signal.

qa.q: What was Pradeep experiencing when he heard Tanuja's words?
qa.a: He was surprised, having believed the silence was meant to punish him, and seemed ready to accept a new way.

grounding: A young woman breaks a week-long freeze by explaining that she goes quiet when overwhelmed and asking to take a break and then come back.

Counselling note, session 3, Lavanya and Bidisha (sisters, sharing a flat in Salt Lake).

Today something shifted. Bidisha had again described the past fortnight as "living with a ghost," and I expected Lavanya to go quiet, as in both earlier sessions.

Instead, after a long pause, Lavanya turned to her sister and said, "When you raise your voice, I go quiet because I'm overwhelmed. It's not that I don't care. Can I take ten minutes when that happens, and then come back?"

Bidisha's eyes filled. She said, "I thought you were punishing me. For two weeks I thought you hated me."

I asked Lavanya how it felt to say it. Lavanya said, "Scary. And lighter."

Plan: at home, Lavanya will use the words "ten minutes" as a signal, and set a timer so the return is visible. We review in a week.

qa.q: What words will Lavanya use at home as a signal?
qa.a: Lavanya will use the words "ten minutes" as a signal.

qa.q: What did Bidisha think Lavanya's silence meant?
qa.a: Bidisha believed the silence was punishment and felt hurt and afraid that Lavanya hated her.

qa.q: Why does explaining the silence make such a difference?
qa.a: Once Lavanya names it as overwhelm and promises to return, the silence becomes a signal Bidisha can trust instead of a weapon.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after saying it aloud?
qa.a: Lavanya felt scared and lighter at the same time, relieved to finally explain.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows one sister explaining her silence as overwhelm and asking for a short break, turning a weapon into a signal.
